newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Halifax makes blue chip market debut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Halifax makes blue chip market debut.

text.p: Britain gained a new blue-chip banking share on Monday when former building society Halifax Plc made its long-awaited, multi-billion pound stock exchange debut.
Halifax expressed satisfaction with the level at which its shares made their mark but analysts were cautious about the price in the longer term, despite strong institutional demand for the new stock.
Nearly two million people will receive windfalls averaging 2,417 pounds ($3,950) after just under a quarter of Halifax shares were sold at 732.5 pence per share at an auction last Friday.
For those who chose not to sell, the shares opened 42 pence higher at 774.5 pence on the stock market but soon lost much of this ground, slipping to 745 by 1000 GMT.

At the average auction price a Halifax shareholder with the maximum share entitlement will have collected 10,116 pounds, while someone with the basic 200 share entitlement will have netted a windfall of 1,465 pounds.
"We hope our members will be delighted with the price," Halifax's head of corporate affairs Gary Marsh told Reuters in an interview. "We are pleased to be able to cement our relationship with them."
Analysts had forecast a high opening price at the auction, although they said the price could have been even higher had there not been a fall in shares in the bank sector on Friday.

"Our analysis suggests that 600-650 pence is about where it should be, based on its fundamental prospects vis a vis other shares in the UK fundamental sector," John Leonard, banking analyst at Salomon Brothers, told Reuters.
"Halifax may be a great company but it is a rich share," said Leonard, who rates the stock a hold.
With a market capitalisation of 18.4 billion pounds at the average auction price, Halifax easily makes the top 10 of Britain's top 100 quoted companies, slotting in at number eight, Marsh said.
The new bank on the block has in fact sneaked in slightly ahead of banking rival Barclays Plc in terms of market capitalisation, he added.
The cash-rich Halifax is widely predicted to give major banks National Westminster Bank Plc, Lloyds TSB, Midland and Barclays a run for their money.

Marsh declined to comment when asked whether Halifax, which has around 20 million customers and more than three billion pounds in cash, would use its new-found flexibility as a public company to make a quick acquisition.
But he repeated that Halifax would consider going on the acquisition trail. "That is one of the options we are looking at," he said.
Halifax's brokers, Merrill Lynch and Cazenove & Co, auctioned around 570 million, 23 percent, of the flotation shares to institutional investors keen to pick up a slice of the huge share handout.
Some 7.6 million Halifax members, those individuals who had saved or borrowed with the 144-year-old society, have become shareholders through the flotation.
Around 1.4 million of these have elected to take share certificates, 1.9 million sold at the first auction and others have taken up the Halifax's offer of a special shareholder account.

The Halifax flotation follows last month's float of the Alliance & Leicester Plc which also ditched its mutual status, where it was owned by its members, in favour of becoming a public limited company.
One analyst, who declined to be named, suggested Halifax shares could rise as high as 800 pence but they would not necessarily stay at this level.
"It's possible the shares will trade up to around eight pounds today. That's not to say we expect it to stay at that level," he said.
Halifax says it is prepared for the trials and tribulations of life as a stock market giant.

"We are pleased we have got the reception we have as a quoted company but this is by no means the end of it for the Halifax. It's the end of one chapter but the beginning of a new one," said Halifax's Marsh.
